title: Chapter 24: Testify or Leave
content: The queue at the Annex is out the door and around the corner, and Hollis Drane is standing at his own window with his coat still on.
Wren puts the envelope on the counter and says, "Notice of witnesses. Two copies. I would like the second one stamped."
"There is a queue."
"There has been a queue since Monday. It is made of people reading my sheets."

"That is not a queue matter." Hollis takes the envelope anyway. He has been taking things from her for sixty-one days, and his hands have got no better at it. "A petitioner representing herself cannot simply file a list."
"Rule twenty-six, section four, paragraph b. A petitioner may appear in person and may call witnesses by notice. It is on the wall behind you, second panel, in the frame with the water stain."
He does not look at the wall. He knows what is on the wall.
He opens the envelope with the letter opener and reads the page, and his mouth moves at the names.
"Aubrey, Wren. Drane, Hollis." He stops. "You have put me on it."
"You took the Form 9s. You put them in the drawer. You are the drawer's keeper and you are going to say so in a room with a stenographer in it."
"I am a clerk."
"You are a witness."
Hollis looks at the page a while longer. Then he says, without lifting his eyes, "You have left off the engineer."
"Yes."
"The survey has his name on it. The review has his name on it. Anybody would call him."
"Anybody would." Wren slides the second copy across. "I am not anybody. Stamp it."
He stamps it slowly, writes the time in pencil, initials it, and pushes it back.
Then he says, "The tray has paper in it."
"What?"
"The out-tray. Second shelf. It has had paper in it since October and nobody has collected it and I am not going to carry it over there myself."
He turns away and calls the next person in the queue. Wren walks down the room to the second shelf.
The top sheet in the tray is a county form, white, face up. She does not have to touch it.
FORM 12. PERSONNEL ACTION.
Employee: Marsh, Theodore R. Classification: Engineer IV, Professional.
Action: transfer. Permanent. District 4 to Center of Engineering, Columbus.
Effective 1 December 2026.
Approved: O. Reeve, Director.
Employee acknowledgment: blank.
The date in the corner of the routing block is 2 October.
Wren reads it four times, which is three times more than it needs, because it is a form and a form does not change.
Six weeks. He has known for six weeks and has not said a word about a form with his whole future typed into a box.
She squares the sheet to the corner of the tray and goes out past the queue without a word.
At noon the diner is loud.
The sheets are up inside the windows now and the light comes through them, so the whole room is the colour of old paper, and people are eating under 1974.
Bram is at the end of the counter with his hands around a cup.
"There is a transfer form in the Annex," Wren says. "Columbus. Effective the first of December."
Bram drinks and puts the cup down and does not look surprised, which is the worst thing he could do.
"He will take it."
"He has not signed the acknowledgment."
"He will take it. Nobody in this room thinks that man is going to stand up on Saturday and say a word against the woman who signs his checks and is mother to the woman he is marrying. Nobody."
"I do."
"Then you are the only one, and you are the one who has to stand up in that room."
Ruthie fills both cups without being asked and says, "The Kessler boy is right and he is being ugly about it," and goes away again.

"I am allowed," Bram says. "My brother went into that water for a child he had never met. That is the whole opinion of the Kessler family on the subject of duty, and it cost us the only one of us who was worth anything."
He says it without trembling. That is how she knows he has said it to himself in the truck.
At four she walks up the gate road.
It is the coldest afternoon yet. The river is low and grey, and the gate sits in its white shed with the road along the top, and behind it the lake she is not allowed to see lies flat and brown.
Theo is on the catwalk below the gate house with a clipboard and a torch, checking the trash rack, because he still has a job until the first of December.
He does not pretend to be surprised.
"You should not be up here."
"I climbed the fence."
He almost laughs and puts the clipboard under his arm.

"The lake is down four feet," he says. "If we do not pulse again by the middle of December the intake takes grit, and the town has brown water for a week, and it is my fault, because everything the water does is my fault now."
"You read the form."
"What form?"
"The Form 12. In the tray. Since the second of October."
"Yes," he says. "I read it."
"Six weeks."

"Six weeks." He turns the torch over in his hand. "She offered it to me in September. The week after the funeral. She drove to my apartment in Columbus and sat in the car and told me there was a position and that she thought I had earned it."
"And you did not take it."
"No."
"Why not?"

"Because taking it in September would have been the same as saying the thing out loud," he says. "There is no paper that says keep quiet. There is a job and a date and everybody understanding. If I had gone then, everybody would have known what it was. Now it is a transfer in a tray and a man who was going to leave anyway." He looks at her. "In April nobody will remember why."
They walk the catwalk to the end and back, and the steel is loud under their boots.

"On Saturday," he says, "I can stand up and say what I signed and what the review says and what the schedule allowed. And then the board opens a complaint, and the complaint goes to the state, and I lose the license. Nine years. Two exams. A master's I am still paying for."
"And if you do not."

"Then I go to Columbus and I am an engineer for the rest of my life and I sign things that other people schedule." He says it evenly. "And in five years there will be a man in this district who signs surveys and does not read the release log, and it will not be me, and I will be in a meeting about silt."
The wind comes up the channel and takes the edge of his coat.
"Ask me," he says.
"No."
"Ask me to stay."
"No."

"Wren." His voice does the thing it did two summers ago, on the boat, at two in the morning, when he told her about the job in Columbus and then told her he was not going to take it. "Ask me. That is all it takes. One sentence and I will be in that room on Saturday with my hand up."
Wren looks at the water.

"If I ask you," she says, "then on Saturday you are doing it for me. And on Sunday you will be a man who lost his license for a woman, and you will hate me in a way that will be very quiet and last thirty years. I have watched my grandfather carry one thing like that. I am not going to hand you another."
"That is not your decision."
"No," she says. "It is not. That is the point. It is yours, and you are the only person in this county who gets to make it, and you have been trying to give it to me all afternoon."
"Then tell me something," he says. "Anything. Tell me why it matters. Not to the county. To you."
Wren thinks about the book in the tin under the counter at the landing, and the four hundred and eleven IOUs in her grandfather's hand.
"He used to say the river does not lie," she says. "It comes up when it comes up. Everything that gets lied about is done on the bank, by people, afterward."
"That is a beautiful thing for a dead man to say."

"He said it for fifty-one years while he was alive. It was not beautiful then either. He said a man who works the water has one job, and the job is to say what the water did. Not what it meant. Not what it cost. What it did."
"If I do this," he says, "I lose the license, and this town will not remember my name in a year."
"There are four thousand names in that book. Nobody remembers any of them. They are still written down."
She leaves him on the catwalk and walks back down the gate road in the dark, and she does not turn around, and the fence is where she left it.
Friday she does not go anywhere.
The table has the log on the left, the Reeve papers in the middle, and the list of forty-one names on the right, typed, in order, with dates.
Four minutes. Two hundred and forty seconds. She has done the arithmetic four times and it comes out different every time, because arithmetic is a comfort and a stopwatch is not.
She reads them out loud.
"Owen Pike, fourteenth of May, nineteen ninety-four." Pause. "Anna Voss Rusk. Harlan Deeds. Deacon Ross. Ada Finch. Walter Nunn."

At the twelfth name her voice does something and she stops and drinks water and starts again from the top, because you do not start in the middle, because starting in the middle is what the county does.

She gets to the fortieth and then there is his name, and she reads it, "Elias Aubrey, twelfth of September, twenty twenty-six," and then she sits with her hands flat on the table until the clock on the wall finishes a minute.
Then she starts again.
At half past four the county calls.
"A new exhibit is in, E-14. Reeve, H., nineteen ninety-eight. Filed this morning at eight forty by Celia Reeve. The petitioner may object. Do you object?"
"No."
"Then it is in." Paper moves. "There is a note in the box for relationship, Miss Aubrey. She has written: niece. Nobody puts that in the box."
"Somebody did."
At six Bram brings two coffees and a bag of Ruthie's sandwiches and sits on the step because the chairs are full of paper.
"He has not called."
"No."
"He is not going to."
"Probably not."
Bram drinks his coffee. Then he says, "Leave the porch light on."
"Why?"

"Because it costs nothing and because I am tired of watching you do arithmetic about people." He stands up and pulls his collar around his neck. "I will be at the courthouse at eight on Saturday. I will sit where you can see me."
At eleven she hears a truck turn off the county road and come down the lane slow, without lights, the way a person drives when he does not want to be seen arriving or to be seen leaving.
The engine stops.
The door does not open.

She stands at the window with her hands on the sill and the yard is black and then not black, because his headlights are off but the instrument panel is on, and it puts a green light on his hands where they sit on the wheel.
He is not getting out.

She can see the shape of him through the windshield, and she can see the passenger seat, and there is a folder on it, and it is thick, and it has the county's blue cover and a label on the front in his own small engineer's hand.
Wren watches for a minute. Then she turns on the porch light and leaves it on and goes back to the table and sits down, and does not lock the door.
highlight: Wren demands a stamped witness notice, and leaves her porch light on for the man who has to choose.
